To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the supply of limited N (2 mM) at Zadok’s scale GS 21 and 31 resulted in reduced tiller survival in spring wheat.
limited N supply at GS 21 resulted 70% less tillers per plant at maturity compared to control.
the tiller production and tiller survival are affected by the limited N supply at different growth stages in wheat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
tiller production and survival under limited N supply at different growth stages in spring wheat.
the influence of limited N supply on tillers per plant at different growth stages.
the effect of limited N supply at specific growth stages on tiller production and tiller abortion process in spring wheat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tillers produced after GS 31 were aborted and the tillers that were produced at GS 21 were the ones that survived and contributed in yield.
the supply of limited N supply after tiller formation (GS 37) did not show significant difference in mature tillers per plant relative to control.
tiller production and survival in wheat are affected by limiting N supply at specific growth stages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tiller abortion process in wheat was initiated after GS 37, but the process was accelerated with limited N supply at GS 31 and GS 21.
limited N supply at early growth stages resulted in tiller abortion and reduced matured tiller production.
tiller survival and development are more susceptible to limited N at early growth stages (GS 21 and GS31).
The main takeaway from our work is that
tiller abortion is not initiated until the plants reach GS 31.
tiller survival and tillering ability are sensitive to N supply at early growth stages and the effect of N deficiency is not reversible.
tiller survival is more sensitive to limited N supply at early growth stages.
